27.t: King Oliver's playing and his gum and teeth trouble
27.s: Oliver played as he had for years but his bridge failed from pyorrhea, so he did not play for about a month in 1933-34 and was not playing well afterward.
27.q: He was playing just like he had been playing for years. Real good and (?) and pretty. He didn't play as high as Louis, but he played up around D and E.

27.t: King Oliver kept to himself and scolded the band for smoking pot
27.s: Oliver didn't socialise or drink and told his players that marijuana made them think they played well.
27.q: No. He used to give us hell for smoking. He'd say, "You all get full of that shit and think you're playing something. You ain't playing a damn thing!" He used to tell the guys that. He said, "You'all sho played sad last night." And we thought we'd played like hell. He said, "You think you played…

27.t: Eating habits ruin Oliver's stomach and his playing declines
27.s: Stories of Oliver's meals, including eating a duck with Louis, and his stomach trouble leading him to miss band dates.
27.q: I remember one time in Chicago (I guess this would have been in the paper; a lot of told it), he used to go in the dressing room with a loaf of bread and sugar. He'd eat that with sugar. He said one time he and Louis eat up a whole duck; in one meal, he and Louis eat the duck up, and didn't have…

27.t: King Oliver as a reluctant front man, his cataract and jealousy
27.s: Oliver stayed behind the band because of a cataract on his eye and was touchy about women in the band.
27.q: there was just certain musicians that could play a show -- Black musicians that could play a show. King said they had him play in the club, but he led the band, took care of the band playing the show. Because King wasn't no kind of a front man. No, he wasn't no front man. He would never get up in…

27.s: Phillips describes Oliver's huge breakfast, six feet tall and around 250 pounds, when he hired them.
27.q: could eat! When we first met him, he called us over to tell us about he wanted us with the band, and how he liked the band and everything. He told us to wait until he got through eating breakfast. When he sat down to eat breakfast, he'd eat a half-a-dozen eggs, a half-a-pound of bacon, and a pot of…

830.t: George Sr. taught Joe Oliver and the string band
830.s: She insists her husband taught Joe Oliver, who played in his brass band and learned string music with his string band; Manuel Manetta also talks about him.
830.ch: Learning music and the early bands
830.q: Well, I just laughed and talked about Joe. We were just talking about Joe. And some of them boys, you know, he taught. Did you say he taught Joe Oliver? He taught Joe. He taught Joe. And many times, he'd give somebody else a present. I'd say, well, they never say nothing about Joe, Steve and Joe.…

830.t: Joe Oliver goes to Chicago; George's own bands
830.s: Joe Oliver went up to Chicago and stayed; she knew him from her house before he married, and George had his own string and brass bands.
830.q: He went up there on physical. Quite a few of the bands were like Joe Oliver, you know, went up there while the guys stayed. Joe went up there all the time and stayed. Joe just had his wife and when Joe left, you know, I don't know if he and his wife was together.

830.t: Credit for bringing out Joe Oliver
830.s: She complains George gets no credit for teaching Oliver, who became famous by leaving for Chicago; the band members chipped in to pay Joe.
830.q: Yes, somebody young. And lots of time when they've given somebody the credit and I often pass it myself. I say, now, George is dead and George brought Joe Oliver out and they don't say anything about him.

837.t: Joe Oliver's white teeth and chewing tar
837.s: A childhood impression of Oliver as a teenager with beautiful white teeth who always chewed a lump of tar.
837.q: Well, let me tell you another memory I have of Joe Oliver that was funny. Although he was only 16 or something like that at the time, if my memory serves me right. He was, I see, much older to a kid who was four years old, five years old. And I was struck by what beautiful white teeth he had. And…

837.t: Oliver's cut shoes, red undershirt and the nickname Monocle
837.s: Oliver slit his new shoes to ease his feet and wore a red undershirt and a derby. He was affectionately called Monocle because of the white eye that bulged when he played.
837.q: I remember Oliver when people wouldn't have remembered him. I remember him with cut shoes. They'd buy a $25 pair of floor charms and cut with a brand new knife there with a knife. They'd cut these new shoes so their feet wouldn't hurt them.

837.t: Oliver's sidemen, sustained notes, Chicago change, and diabetes
837.s: Souchon names sidemen and says no record shows Oliver's single sustained note. In Chicago Oliver had changed his style and added saxes. Ory's West Coast group came closest to the old sound. Souchon suspects Oliver had diabetes.
837.q: Exactly the same way. The personnel of the band was something that was interesting, too. I remember Ori playing with them. I remember Johnny Dodds. I don't remember Baby Dodds playing with them. If he did, I don't remember it. Bob Foster played with them sometimes. And then what's this other bass…

418.t: Amos Gilliat, the toothless trombone virtuoso, and King Oliver selling clams
418.s: Dickenson tells of a ragged trombonist who played an exercise book flawlessly without teeth, and of seeing King Oliver selling clams in Savannah.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: I was with Zack White's band. Zack White's band. And we went to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and we were at some hotel there. Some third class hotel -- fourth class hotel or something.

418.t: Amos Giliad, the toothless trombone virtuoso, and King Oliver selling clams
418.s: Dickenson tells of a ragged trombonist in Harrisburg who played an exercise book flawlessly without teeth, and of seeing King Oliver selling clams in Savannah.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Oh yeah! I was with Zack Whyte's band, and we went to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. And we were at some hotel there, some third-class hotel or fourth-class hotel or something... You know, we didn't have no money hardly, just scuffling, you know. And here comes this guy, and he was real raggedy, you…

418.t: Amos Gilliad, the toothless trombone virtuoso, and King Oliver selling clams
418.s: Dickenson tells of a ragged trombonist in Harrisburg who played an exercise book flawlessly without teeth, and of seeing King Oliver selling clams in Savannah.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: I was with Zack White's band. Zack White's band. And we went to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania and we were at some hotel there. Some third class hotel -- fourth class hotel or something. You know, we didn't have no money hardly. Scuffling you know. And here comes this guy. And he was real raggedy you…

248.s: Oliver first could only play brass band music; Dawson hired a substitute for a dance; Oliver later became a fine sight reader and left with Armstrong.
248.ch: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
248.q: When, uh, Oliver, Joe Oliver, when I first got Joe Oliver, he only could play brass band music. He couldn't play no dance music. He had a, he had a, uh, a shoe shop uptown repairing shoes. Joe did that? Joe Oliver. He didn't know any of them. Yeah, and I, I went to hire him to play a dance up on…

248.t: King Oliver dropping a brick to signal the band to stop
248.s: Dawson explains Oliver threw a brick on the music stand to cut off players who ran past the knock-off; the hall was uptown, name forgotten.
248.q: What was that for? That was for the, to give you a notice to stop playing, you know. When you, the boys when they knock off, they keep on playing over, you know, couple of strings, couple of bars over the beat, over the knockoff and well, he just got a big brick and when he got ready to knock off…

259.t: Joe Oliver and the early Kid band
259.s: He knew Joe Oliver, older by five or six years, who came up in a youngsters' brass band and later led his own; he recalls Oliver's wife Stella and Armstrong leaving with him.
259.ch: Mexico trip and Charlie Tolles band
259.q: Did you know Joe Oliver? Oh yeah, Joe. He was on the corner from Joe Oliver. That's the time I used to go to the Royal Guard. He got that job out today. Bless you know. Yeah, he was the king out there. And then when he was older than me, he was about five or six years old than me. But I know them…

259.t: Buddy Sali, the drummer who hit Joe Oliver
259.s: Vincent confirms that drummer Buddy Sali was the one who hit Joe Oliver. Sali played a while afterward but died young of consumption.
259.q: Buddy Salo. Buddy Salo? Yeah. That's the one that hit Joe Lewis. Joe Oliver. Yeah. And what Joe Lewis? Joe Oliver. Oliver. Joe Oliver.

706.s: Armstrong says Oliver took time to show young musicians passages while others were too busy at the Eagle Saloon.
706.ch: Joe Oliver and the second line
706.q: I love Joe because he's taking more time with the other musicians. I noticed they all were so busy going to the Eagle Saloon. And I feel a boy, he might say, well, would you show me how this passage goes, you know, you're a little stuck with this division. Oh boy, I ain't got time to be bothered…

706.t: Admiring Oliver and playing second cornet
706.s: Armstrong says it was a big thing to be sent for by Oliver, whom he admired; he had few solos and did not yet sing.
706.q: There were like one or two records, I think it was chimes, blues, or something like that. But I never wanted to do that in Oval Joe. Did you sing at all? No. That came later? Yeah. Because he knew I was singing, but the main thing was to kind of play with him. And I was singing in a little quartet…

12.t: Replacing Buster Bailey; Oliver as leader
12.s: Rudy Jackson and Nicholas in the band; Oliver's stock arrangements and insistence on blended, controlled playing.
12.q: That first album? Oh, I don't know. Let's see. He had, well, mostly, we had stock arrangements and just a little skeleton move. Mm-hmm. Just to keep you together, you know. Mm-hmm. Big Randy like now. Mm-hmm. But he liked his music. Joe was pretty clever. And he liked to hear everybody in the band.…

12.t: Johnny Dodds's originality and knowing King Oliver
12.s: Dodds stood apart in sound and fingering; Nicholas replaced Dodds in 1924 and knew Oliver from New Orleans brass bands.
12.q: I took Johnny Dodds' place in 24. I knew King Oliver when I was a kid, around New Orleans, playing second trumpet in the brass band with Manuel Perez, an onward brass band. Then I played with King Oliver a couple of times before I went into the Navy, when I was around 16 and 17 years of age. Joe…

128.t: King Oliver and learning by stealing
128.s: Brief talk of King Oliver, and Jim says he learned by listening and stealing from other players.
128.q: No, no. King Oliver was a man listening, playing music, long listening. Came up and playing music, long. See, I just listened. I taught in tramo in 1970. Them people had been playing. And Poetsy? That's right. People had been playing, man. And I learned fast. Because I stole what I got. I stole…

128.t: Kid Ory's band on the Cabaret Hall front porch
128.s: Ory played trombone with Oliver on Monday nights on a hall's front porch, and Robinson remembers the trombonists then.
128.q: Every, every Monday night with Kid Oliver. Uh, right when I checked that right there now on, uh, on, uh, Tremont Street. Every Monday night, Kiddawa would play every Monday night, you know. Kiddawa was playing trombone. They had a front porch. The front porch, the band would come out on the evening…

15.t: King Oliver as a leader and his enormous appetite
15.s: Howard calls Oliver businesslike and comical, easy to work for, and describes his huge meals and home life.
15.q: No trouble whatsoever. Yeah. A lot of foolishness. I mean, he was strictly business on the job, but he was comical, you know, do things, make you laugh. I had no trouble with a very fine guy to work with.

15.t: Last seeing Oliver in 1937 and the dozens story at rehearsal
15.s: Howard saw a sick Oliver in Nashville in 1937 and tells how Oliver reacted when Barney kept asking him to turn on his stand light.
15.q: Street clothes. You know, remember I told you they went on the change clothes? Yeah, that's why I was asking you. Well, Joe wore tuxedos, that band wore tuxedo early. See, later on I went down to Warwick's club, Wallace Tyler's place, and worked with King Oliver. And then later on, that's when Jean…

9.t: King Oliver in the studio, sick and silent
9.s: Oliver attended the recording dates but never played; Holmes found it a letdown and says Oliver was at the end of the line with bad gums.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: : Yeah, he would be in the studio. I mean, he wasn't doing anything. He was just there. He had nothing to say. If there was anything said, he would say it to Russell or the technicians or something. He had nothing to say to the band or anything.

9.t: Hearing King Oliver's band at the Savoy, with Red Allen
9.s: Oliver fronted his Savoy band without playing while Red Allen did the trumpet work, and the band broke up and mostly returned to Chicago.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: : even. I hadn't even heard of him before. And I didn't know him or anything like that... But he was standing up in featured in the band, he did all the trumpet work. And I expected to hear King Oliver play, but he wasn't playing. His teeth were bad or something -- he was having trouble.

95.t: Joe Oliver's house, his sponsoring her trips, his death and "Caldonia"
95.s: She visited Oliver's home in Chicago, he handled her songs and advised on her fee, and she says he died of ptomaine poisoning from sardines, costing her money for "Caldonia".
95.q: He was (inaudible) and he was getting the money (unintelligible) Sippie Walker (unintelligible) and told me, says, "Sippie, (unintelligible)." But see, I thought (unintelligible). But I'd have been glad to get $5,000, you know. But Joe told me, says, "Don't ask for no $5,000."

95.s: She remembers Joe Oliver as easy to get along with and gentle with a young girl.
95.q: Well, that's all I ever knew about Joe because I was kind of halfway scared of his wife and him being such a gentleman, because I was really , you know. (Unintelligible) go on home to my brother or to my cousin's family.

859.t: Armstrong's last dance, Sidney Desvigne's band and King Oliver
859.s: Gabriel recalls Armstrong's farewell dance in 1923, playing drums in Sidney Desvigne's band, and King Oliver rehearsing with his father.
859.q: And the last thing Louis played was a dance for my daddy at the Coliseum. I advertised, not the dance. He played the advertised. I played the clarinet. He left that same night in 1923. First time a dance was ever gave down there. But Sidney Dazman, he played the job. And I played with Sidney…

689.t: Joe Oliver as a fun-loving man; his wife and death
689.s: Oliver was full of jokes, played opposite Dominique and Louis in Chicago cabarets; talk of his wife, daughter and where he died.
689.q: Fine fella. Swell guy. Full of fun. I work right opposite. Louie and I work opposite. And don't think, cause Louie and I was across the street. Joe Oliver had Bob Schauffer. And he also had Kid Ory. He had Joyce Field there, too. He had Kid Ory with him. Don't think the plantation was packed. Like…

646.t: Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong in Chicago, 1917
646.s: The man recalls Joe Oliver and Armstrong going to Chicago, registering for the Army there in 1917, and Oliver's fame and records.

773.t: How her husband started drumming; Bechet and Joe Oliver
773.s: He began beating sticks on his mother's bed; early band with Armstrong, Bechet unreliable, Joe Oliver, and her photograph of Oliver.
773.ch: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
773.q: Well, he started, uh, he told me he used to take two sticks, you know, drumsticks. And his mother had one of them wooden bits. And that's how he started beating drums on the back of the bed. And he used to say, I know, put them sticks down. His mother would get after him by putting the sticks down.…

35.t: Bunk on Joe Oliver and the tune Please
35.s: Bunk said nothing notable on Oliver; Blumberg recalls Please as one of Bunk's most lyrical tunes.
35.q: I think, I mean, I think that he just said the same thing, yeah, Oliver was a wonderful trumpet player, or something like that, but, uh, Aside from that, nothing. Nothing.

816.t: Hearing King Oliver and Kid Ory
816.s: Warner danced to Oliver at Economy Hall and liked Ory's tone, though he was not yet interested in music.
816.q: Oh yeah, I used to go dance by Oliver's music. He used to play around here at the economy hall. Yeah, I used to be at him and, was that the fellow here in California now, Kid Ori? Ori? Yeah. That's when Oliver left here. I was at the last dance he played over at the economy hall.

252.t: Royal Garden in Chicago: Professor Jones, King Oliver, Lil and Louis
252.s: Laurena recalls the emcee Jones and the King Oliver band with Lil, Louis Armstrong and Tubby Hall.
252.q: Well, now, they had Lil Armstrong. She wasn't a Lil Armstrong then. I don't know what her name, but later on she married Louis. And King Oliver had the band there then. And Louis was on the, I should say the second trumpet, because King Oliver played the, you know, he was on the first trumpet, I…

126.t: New Orleans music on return: Piron, Robichaux, Oliver and Monocle
126.s: Back in New Orleans he heard Piron, Robichaux, King Oliver and a five-piece band led by a pop-eyed cornetist; Oliver left for Chicago about September.
126.q: In New Orleans? Well, I took up where we left off. Uh, Pierron was still playing, and Robichell was still playing, and they had King Oliver, if you remember him. He was playing that, man. We attended a lot of the musical extravaganzas he put on. And then there was a band, I don't know what the name…

775.t: King Oliver, Louis Armstrong and the Royal Garden on Rampart Street
775.s: He remembers Oliver taking young Armstrong on parades, a raid on the Royal Garden after which Louis took over the band, and the band's lineup.
775.q: Yeah, I remember King Oliver. That's the time, I remember when he used to take Louis Armstrong on parades, during the First World War. Louis was in short pants then. And, uh, and I remember when, uh, Joe Oliver used to play at the Royal Garden, at it on Ramport Street. I remember the night he, he,…

151.t: Blue Mondays in 1948 and King Oliver's decline
151.s: Reason recalls hosting Oliver's wife and the later health decline of Oliver, who told him he was the last New Orleans musician he would send for.
151.ch: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
151.q: And, um, but, uh, um, when I saw Stella, she used to come to my house. With this drummer, um, they used to, they used to take around quite often to see the town and, uh, they used to come to my house. I was living on Liberty, uh, uh, Irana and Liberty. My people used to own that corner. And we used…

46.t: Joe Oliver, Keppard and Hightower's pleasure ground
46.s: He recalls holding Joe Oliver's plantation job after Oliver's fall, and compares his friendship with Oliver to his business ties to Keppard.
46.ch: Hightower: New Orleans parades and early players
46.q: Well, it's just like one of those things that, that I figured that although that me and Joe turned out to be the best friend, and when he got sick here on his last laps, I held his job down at the plantation for him for about six months, and did my work too, because he was unable to work. You see,…

714.t: Chicago blues-era New Orleans players: Tony Jackson and Joe Oliver
714.s: Dorsey says he knew Tony Jackson and Joe Oliver, with whom he played the same cabaret; Oliver was a bigger man who might not notice him.
714.q: He's gone. He's gone. He's a bigger man. He might not have seen you. He was called Bad Eyes in the stuff. Did you know Louis? Yeah, Joe was great.

281.t: Oliver's Lincoln Gardens band, Armstrong and sitting in
281.s: He heard Oliver's band with the Doddses, Lil Hardin and Armstrong, sat in on Dippermouth Blues, and describes Johnny Dodds.
281.q: Well, it was Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and I think so. I think Sincere was in the band. I think a bass player by the name of Johnson.

665.t: Joe Oliver as a butler on Second and Magazine
665.s: She worked as house girl where Joe Oliver was a butler, and describes his leaving with a band.
665.q: Right there with him. He had one bad eye. I don't know if it was out, but it was swole out. You know, big eye they used to call him. And them wifey was crazy about him. He left from here. When music got good or waste, he had went away with a band somewhere and things was good there. And he left…

777.t: Hearing the Olympia band and Edward Clem
777.s: Williams heard the Olympia and trumpeter Edward Clem, a non-reading jazz player of the blues, who visited his home area.
777.ch: Early New Orleans music and Mardi Gras
777.q: He was doing officer work for the dance. Something I wanted to ask you about was who were some of the other bands that you heard when you were quite young, like out in the country, who did you hear that come out there from the city? Well, I heard the Olympia. Mm-hmm.

778.t: When she came to New Orleans in 1920
778.s: Joe Oliver's visit came about a month before she moved in warm 1920; billiard gardens were running.
778.q: It was spring or summertime. It was spring or not spring time. Because they had all the bill guards running in New Orleans. It was warm. It was warm. It was 1920 it was nice and warm.

648.t: Dixieland combination versus older Black orchestras; competition
648.s: Brown's band was a pioneer; Oliver and Armstrong's earlier bands were larger with violins; only Fisher's band competed.
648.ch: Brown's Band and Tom in Chicago
648.q: He deserved credit. Well, he was, in reality, a pioneer in the jazz field. And there was other colored bands that were up there. This was before Louis Armstrong came up there. This was before King Oliver and all those came up. King Oliver and the bands that King Oliver played, and Armstrong, when…

5.t: Oliver's recordings, and sitting in at Dreamland
5.s: He thinks Oliver's few records do not do him justice and says he sat in with him at the Dreamland.
5.q: He, well I tell you, I don't think he, I've never heard, I've never heard, heard many recordings of Joe and what recordings that he made. I didn't, didn't, uh, I don't think it, it, it gives him, you know.

290.t: Parade bands, Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong, and the shortage of players
290.s: He played with Oliver and Armstrong in parade bands; bands were always short of men, so almost anyone who could play got work and swapped between bands.
290.q: Yeah, yeah, I know Joe Oliver. I know him, I might say well, I played in bands with him, parade bands, you know. Yeah. I know him.

881.t: Roy Palmer as teacher; the New Orleans clique and Oliver's band split
881.s: He hears Roy Palmer at his mother's fish fries, lists Palmer's pupils, and explains how the New Orleans musicians in Chicago fell out over Oliver's recordings.
881.q: Yeah. Well, sometime my mother would have a fish fry and she was engaged with Roy Palmer. He had a friend that played a mountain. Later on you know Roy Palmer played baritone, cornet, trombone, a lot of instruments. He was a pretty good teacher. He taught a lot of people around Chicago, including…

292.t: King Oliver, lake camps and vaudeville with bands
292.s: King Oliver as first Negro jazz band, jazz at the lake camps by phonograph, and vaudeville houses that had bands before talkies.
292.q: Oh, they used to have the old time radios out there with the horns. If they didn't have a band, they would have a radio with a big horn. I mean a phonograph and would have the records. Did you see King Oliver yourself? No, I've heard of him.

573.t: Most popular bands then, and a goodbye
573.s: Joe Oliver had a tough band; Morgan says they played picnics, then the interviewers briefly sign off.
573.q: It becomes Fess. Joe Oliver had a, a, a tough band. Was Ori playing much then? Well yeah, I, I was, I used to, I used to hire men. I used to play them picnics up there with us until he, until he, until he moved. We're just about two here.

296.t: Joe Oliver leads the Onward band; Labor Day parade
296.s: Oliver took over the Onward band when Perez left for Chicago; the band played a colored Labor Day parade.
296.q: Uh. Joe Oliver. Mm-hmm. Joe Oliver led the band when the 9th Paris went to Chicago. You see? Mm-hmm. And he took charge of the band. He was playing second trumpet, you know? Mm-hmm. So when 9th went away, he led the band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Eddie Jackson was playing football.

270.t: Father's stories about Joe Oliver working on the riverfront
270.s: His father knew Joe Oliver, who lived on Fort Street c. 1915, worked on the riverfront for white employers who let him play weekends, and bought his first cornet that way.
270.q: My daddy knew Joe Oliver very well. He used to always tell me about Joe Oliver, how he was, uh, he used to eat so much, and how he was bragging on how much coffee and things he could drink always more than anybody. And, uh, I remember one time that he told me he was staying on 4th Street. And that…

56.s: They discuss Oliver's poverty and death, and Louis not knowing many numbers.
56.q: Yeah. I don't know. I'd love Joe the good old boy to play.

909.t: Bebe Ridgely, Zoo Robertson, Roy Palmer and Frankie Dusen
909.s: Morris answers about trombonists and cornetists Ridgely, Zoo, Palmer and Oliver's band, and says Dusen worked with everyone and ran the Pelican place.
909.q: Yeah, I remember Bebe Ridgely. That's when they put the pelican up. Bebe Ridgely had that over in charge, when the pelican used to be there. He used to play that.

1038.t: Johnny Dodds and Jelly Roll Morton known in France
1038.s: The French know Armstrong and Bechet, but King Oliver and Johnny Dodds are little known and hard to find; Morton is better known.
1038.q: Oh, he is very few known. In fact, the French people know the big names, that's to say Armstrong, obviously, Bichet, because he is here in France. But they know King Oliver very few, and Johnny Dodds, I don't think, but there are only some fans, some specialists who they know. And we have a lot of…

1.t: King Oliver and Armstrong leaving: the second trumpet tradition
1.s: Barker says there was no bitterness when Armstrong left Joe Oliver, explaining the New Orleans tradition of a second trumpet.
1.q: Oh, that's not no bitterness. I don't think there was no, there was no bitterness, but it was a sort of a, a loss to Joe because there was a tradition in New Orleans to have two trumpets in the band. Papa Celestine had two, at one time, Manny Perez had two, first and second trumpet. And, uh, other…

177.t: Oliver Giles and Kid Bush's band
177.s: Oliver played in different city bands, with Kid Bush among those named.
177.q: Who did he play with? Well he played with different bands in the city, he played here in the Orleans. A fellow they called Bush, Kid Bush, I don't know if you ever heard of him. You see a long time ago that's the way they used to call bands.

783.t: Working with Joe Oliver: humour and relaxing the band
783.s: Shoffner says Oliver was easy to work with, joked constantly, and had the band repeat one number until relaxed before making it.
783.q: Well the whole time I find that Joe was just like you say. Joe was an easy fellow to get along with. And he never did let you get tense. He never let you get tense. Yeah. Because he was joking the whole night long. That's what most people tell me. He just kept you in a good mood. You never got…

639.t: Hearing Joe Oliver at Tulane Gym
639.s: He first heard Oliver at the Saturday dances around 1917 and describes the sound that held him spellbound.
639.q: Oh, I think it was around 1917 at Tulane Gym. They gave subscription dances every Saturday night at Tulane Gym. And every time they could get him, they got him. Yeah. And they got him for everything else they could get him for too. He had the cream of the crop. He had Kidore on trombone, Johnny…

905.t: Henry Zeno and King Oliver with the big eye
905.s: Mrs. Phillips' cousin Zeno drummed in the Eagle Band; they discuss Oliver, his eye, and musicians who followed him.
905.q: When he was done, he played with Tuxedo. I know. That's when he died. He played with Tuxedo. But I, about 32 cents I've been in New York. I ain't never here about a drummer. That's interesting. Yes, that's interesting. Oh, everybody used to talk somewhat about that boy. Father did, too. That's why…

833.t: Joe Oliver, where the Dodds lived, and where Robinson lived on Third Street
833.s: He did not know Joe Oliver; they discuss where the Dodds lived, and he says he first lived on Third Street.
833.ch: Early New Orleans recording bands and Third Street
833.q: I always planned to talk of it Joe Oliver but this Johnny Dodd and that little baby Dodd I know good. Remember where they lived in those days about where did they live? No I didn't I think it's uptown somewhere but I never did know. I'm not sure either I know one time baby lived up around

26.t: King Oliver's band at the Savoy
26.s: Greer says he first met Oliver and Barney Bigard when the band came to the Savoy, but he never listened to other bands.
26.ch: The Washingtonians, Bechet and drum style
26.q: Not when I was there, no. They came to New York. They came to the Savoy. We were in New York then. We were at the Cotton Club then. That's the first time. That's the first time I met King and Barney. Barney was with them, lot of guys. That's the first time we met Barney.

87.s: He saw Joe Oliver's band before Oliver went to Chicago; Louis was not with him then.
87.q: And they'd come through there. Joe Oliver would come through Savannah. But Joe Oliver -- when I knew Joe Oliver was coming through there -- Louis wasn't with Joe Oliver at that particular time.

68.t: Hearing King Oliver in Oklahoma City
68.s: Tate compares Oliver's records with Armstrong's, and hears him declining in person at a ballroom with a big band.
68.q: Okay. Well, when -- this is after I joined the band. Well, King Oliver, I had listened to King Oliver's records and I would listen to Louie and he didn't move me like Louie. He could play, but this was before he developed pyorrhea and all of that. He could play, but his sound wasn't as fat and he…

146.t: Never meeting King Oliver; Duke Huddleson
146.s: Smith knew King Oliver only from records and says tenorist Duke Huddleson is a friend who recorded.
146.ch: Later views and life in Dallas
146.q: Yeah. We missed him all the time. Like (?) and (?). We missed them all the time. They stayed back down in this part of the country, and went back out through the Mississippi and all down through there...

167.s: Bunn heard Joe Oliver play but did not sit in with his groups.
167.q: The way he played to me was all right with me at that time. As I got older and the music commenced to get older, it sounded a little different, but every time I'd hear him, he sounded the same.

117.t: King Oliver's decline and the need to read
117.s: Freeman knew Louis and Earl but not Oliver, whose last job he heard was racking balls in a poolroom, and notes soloists could not make a living.
117.q: Yes, and he was going -- of course, poor King Oliver stayed around Chicago a couple of years and -- well, you know more about this because you have gone into research, and then went down south and the last I heard he was working in a poolroom racking up balls. It was sad, this great genius who had…

18.t: What King Oliver's band was called
18.s: JCH knows only that it was King Oliver's band.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: They said he was the greatest, one of the greatest trumpet players but I don't know nothing else about him -- just King Oliver's band.

94.t: Kid Ory and King Oliver not heard
94.s: Moore says he heard nothing of Kid Ory in those years; everything was Armstrong.
94.q: No, I didn't hear anything about Kid Ory. Everything was Armstrong, Armstrong. And then at one time, I heard of King Oliver, and also. But I didn't a, I didn't get the chance to. I think Ory was in a, in California. He always -- when he left New Orleans, I think he went straight

72.t: How he came to join King Oliver through Dave Nelson
72.s: Moore played the Nest Club with Dave Nelson, Oliver's nephew, who introduced him; Oliver ran a business-like band, 1929 to about 1937.
72.ch: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
72.q: The Nest Club. That was on 133rd Street. I started working there around five, I'd get out of there at eleven the next day. Play eight shows. People from downtown used to come up there. The place was packed every night. We'd come out of there with something... I was making forty dollars a week, and…

13.t: Johnny and Baby Dodds, and hearing King Oliver
13.s: Wilson calls Johnny Dodds quiet and Baby jokey, heard Oliver at the Mahjong but never played with him.
13.q: No, I heard them when they was at the Mahjong, across the street from Sunset.

79.s: While on tour with Claude Hopkins, Thomas met King Oliver at Tybee Beach near Savannah, and later told Pops about it.
79.ch: Louis Armstrong, King Oliver and St. Louis memories
79.q: He was by himself. They were doing things like they'd thank come out of town, than you, Baby, they'd come out of town. They'd come from Chicago. They might have been working with -- I don't know. No, I think it was Carol Dickerson's band but they might have been working with Joe Oliver during that…
